scope: Nineteenth expansion batch: 12 controlled verb-form exercises. Three newly possible actions contrast with three new habitual actions before printed you-ni narimashita. Three positive maintained practices contrast with three negative maintained practices before printed you-ni shiteimasu. The article explains change versus deliberate practice, but these supplied-pattern blanks do not independently test selecting naru versus suru in an unrestricted context.

sources.publisher: The Japan Foundation, Minna no Kyozai
sources.section: Actual HTML heading Vようになります, structure chart and explanations A/B: dictionary verbs for changed habits and potential verbs for changed ability or circumstances. Examples include both efforts/study and changed access conditions. Explanation C teaches Vなくなります for cessation of a previous habit or situation. The teacher note's categorical restrictions and old JLPT labels are not generalized beyond this elementary pattern.

sources.publisher: The Japan Foundation, Minna no Kyozai
sources.section: Actual HTML heading Vようにします: dictionary/negative forms, explanation A for conscious effort to do or not do, B for habitual effort with you-ni shiteimasu. The teacher notes contrast a decision with koto-ni suru and explicitly set aside a separate purpose/result-arrangement use of you-ni suru; the volitional-verb restriction belongs to the scoped effort use, not every construction ending you-ni suru.

Potential-form explanation, section 1 group 1: replace the final u of the dictionary form with eru. Applied here to yomu, noru and hanasu. This batch does not depend on group-2 ra-dropping or the page's register judgment about it.

Main lesson describing effort and the corresponding negative-verb avoidance use. Used as supplementary support for conscious effort, not as evidence that every apparent habitual success is guaranteed or for the literal-etymological explanation in its Fun Fact.

authoringNotes: All scenarios are original. Source patterns and structure charts do not automatically establish the naturalness or complete answer set of a new sentence; independent linguistic review remains necessary.

The first six questions explicitly request the given verb's dictionary or potential form, without extra words. The same three verbs occur on both sides. All six print you-ni narimashita, so the past ending cannot decide between ability and habit. The question-visible English selects the intended focus, not an answer-only inference.

The larger-display item is newly available possibility due to deliberately changed conditions. The bicycle item involves practiced skill, and the French item limits the resulting ability to simple matters. Naru does not require an unintentional or universally gradual change. The three habitual items establish prior ability and describe a new regular behavior; do not claim every alternative possibility reading is globally ungrammatical.

The latter six questions request the supplied verb's dictionary or nai form before printed you-ni shiteimasu. Yomu, tsukau and hanasu occur in both directions. The negative lies within the behavior deliberately avoided, not on the effort itself. The smartphone item admits lapses; maintained effort does not guarantee perfect performance. The stairs and disclosure items retain the contextual limits of the practice.

The article inventory was screened. Koto-ni suru can express a decision to start a practice, tsumori can express intention, and suitable purpose/effort or change paraphrases can describe the same situation. They are not globally wrong; the visible verb-form task and already printed construction keep them outside these particular blanks. Mixed contextual selection remains a later planned task.

Both Japanese prompts and English form/focus instructions are visible before answering. Explanations explicitly distinguish requested focus from absolute grammatical impossibility. Only the missing verb form is accepted, in kana or the ordinary kanji spelling; the printed you phrase is not repeated in acceptedAnswers.

The naru/suru distinction is taught in the learner article, not counted as a separately tested contrast in these items. Similarly the article's cessation example uses naku naru; no claim is made that the positive-change exercises cover lost abilities, ended habits, indirect instructions or wishes.

The two JPF URLs were known actual lesson IDs from the previously inspected grammar index. Simplified retrieval again returned only helpfulness counters, so the actual HTML headings, charts, examples and teacher notes were inspected using a text parser.

Supplementary https://bunpro.jp/grammar_points/ようになる was inspected, but its potential-only attachment statement is not adopted because the JPF chart and habitual examples explicitly support dictionary verbs. Its negative-attachment guidance differs from the JPF elementary warning; no universal claim banning Vnai-you-ni-naru is made. The separate attempted Bunpro you-ni-shiteiru URL returned404 and is not evidence.

All245 prior exercise records and identities remain unchanged. The article gains a scoped subsection and one reference bullet; only the preceding transition sentence is updated to point to the new subsection instead of saying change/effort practice is still needed. One SRS identity per exercise regardless of spelling or presentation.
